plain.Vitamin C is also an important physiolog: Vitamin C protects your body from damage caused by free radicals, and it can “recharge” vitamin E so vitamin E can keep working.
plain.Vitamin E is a fat-soluble antioxidant t: Vitamin E dissolves in fat. When fats in your body react with oxygen, harmful molecules called ROS (reactive oxygen species) can form. Vitamin E helps stop that.
plain.Selenium is a constituent of 25 selenopr: Selenium is a building block of 25 proteins in your body. Some of them, like glutathione peroxidases, are enzymes that help clean up harmful molecules.
plain.It is required for the catalytic activit: Zinc helps hundreds of enzymes do their jobs. It supports your immune system, making proteins and DNA, wound healing, and cells communicating and dividing.
plain.In addition, defense against oxidative d: Your body’s defense against oxygen damage relies mostly on SOD enzymes that contain copper.
plain.Manganese is a cofactor for many enzymes: Manganese is a helper that many enzymes need to work, including the SOD enzyme in your mitochondria (SOD2).
plain.A stable and sensitive measure of ribofl: A lab test called EGRAC checks whether you are low in riboflavin (vitamin B2). It measures how well an enzyme in red blood cells works with and without extra B2 added in the test tube.
plain.Another folate-dependent reaction, the m: Folate is needed to make one of the building blocks of DNA. Without it, cells can’t divide properly.
plain.Vitamin B12 is required for the developm: Vitamin B12 is needed for your brain and nerves to develop and work (including their protective coating, myelin), to make healthy red blood cells, and to make DNA.
plain.Vitamin C is required for the biosynthes: Your body needs vitamin C to make collagen (a protein in skin, tendons and blood vessels), carnitine, and some brain chemical messengers. It also helps process protein.
plain.You need protein in your diet to help yo: Eating protein gives your body what it needs to fix cells and build new ones.
plain.However, clinical trials have reported a: In studies, high-dose vitamin E pills were linked to a higher chance of a stroke caused by bleeding in the brain.
plain.High doses of supplemental iron (45 mg/d: Taking 45 mg or more of iron a day from supplements can upset your stomach, for example causing nausea or constipation.
plain.For this reason, the FNB concluded that: Experts decided that people who smoke need 35 mg more vitamin C each day than people who don’t.
plain.The results from large clinical trials i: Big studies found that a specific supplement mix (called AREDS) slows an eye disease of aging, macular degeneration, in people at high risk of the advanced form. It is not shown to prevent it in everyone.
plain.The data for antioxidant capacity of foo: Test-tube “antioxidant scores” for foods don’t tell us what happens in the human body, and studies of antioxidants in people have had mixed results. So the USDA removed its ORAC antioxidant table.
plain.Antioxidants protect cells from the dama: Free radicals are unstable molecules with an unpaired electron that can damage cells. Antioxidants help protect cells from them.
plain.The body forms ROS endogenously when it: Your body naturally makes ROS (reactive oxygen species) when it turns food into energy. Antioxidants may help protect your cells from them.
plain.Reductions in erythrocyte copper-zinc su: Taking about 60 mg of zinc a day for up to 10 weeks has been linked to lower copper-zinc SOD in red blood cells, a sign that too much zinc can lower your copper.
plain.Other carotenoids in food, such as lycop: Some plant pigments, like lycopene, lutein and zeaxanthin, don’t turn into vitamin A, but they may still do other useful things in the body.
plain.Food and Drug Administration has require: Some medicines you swallow carry an FDA warning not to have grapefruit or grapefruit juice with them. Check your medicine’s label or ask a pharmacist.
plain.However, the ATBC trial found that suppl: In large studies, people who smoke (or had asbestos exposure) and took high-dose beta-carotene pills had more lung cancer and deaths. These high doses are not recommended for them.
plain.In a follow-up analysis of 3,882 of the: Five years after a study ended, people who had taken the version with beta-carotene still had a higher lung cancer risk (82% higher). Newer versions use lutein and zeaxanthin instead.
plain.Superoxide dismutases (SODs) are univers: SOD is a helper protein (enzyme) that living things using oxygen make themselves. It turns superoxide, a very reactive “free radical”, into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide.
plain.The catalase (CAT), glutathione peroxida: Hydrogen peroxide is then handled by other enzymes, catalase and glutathione peroxidases (and peroxiredoxins), which turn it into water.
plain.The Cu/Zn SOD SOD1 is the cytoplasmic is: SOD1 uses copper and zinc and works mainly in the fluid inside cells (the cytoplasm).
plain.The Mn SOD SOD2 localizes to the mitocho: SOD2 uses manganese and works inside mitochondria, the cell’s energy factories, where a lot of superoxide is made.
plain.The Cu/Zn SOD SOD3 is secreted into the: SOD3 also uses copper and zinc, but it is sent outside cells, into the spaces between them and fluids like blood.
plain.Oral administration of protein is very c: SOD is a protein. Proteins you swallow tend to be broken down in the stomach and gut, so an SOD pill is unlikely to arrive in your cells as working SOD. Your body makes its own SOD; what it needs from food is copper, zinc and manganese.
plain.Vitamin A is the name of a group of fat-: Vitamin A is a family of fat-soluble compounds (mainly retinol). It helps your immune system, communication between cells, growth, and reproduction.
plain.Vitamin C, also known as L-ascorbic acid: Vitamin C dissolves in water. Unlike most animals, people can’t make it, so you must get it from food or supplements.
plain.Vitamin D (also referred to as calcifero: Vitamin D is fat-soluble. A few foods have it, some have it added, and your skin makes it when sunlight (UV rays) hits it.
plain.Vitamin E is found naturally in some foo: “Vitamin E” is the name for a group of fat-soluble compounds that act as antioxidants.
plain.Vitamin K, the generic name for a family: Vitamin K is a family of fat-soluble compounds with a shared chemical shape: K1 (from plants) and K2 (a group called menaquinones).
plain.Thiamin (or thiamine) is one of the wate: Thiamin is vitamin B1, one of the B vitamins that dissolve in water.
plain.Riboflavin (also known as vitamin B2) is: Riboflavin is vitamin B2, a water-soluble B vitamin found in some foods, added to others, and sold as a supplement.
plain.Niacin (also known as vitamin B3) is one: Niacin is vitamin B3. The name covers several related forms, such as nicotinic acid and nicotinamide.
plain.Pantothenic acid (also known as vitamin: Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) is a water-soluble vitamin you need from food. Its main job is helping make coenzyme A, a helper molecule used in many reactions.
plain.Vitamin B6 is a water-soluble vitamin th: “Vitamin B6” is the name for six closely related compounds that all work as B6. It dissolves in water.
plain.Biotin, a B vitamin, is an essential nut: Biotin is a water-soluble B vitamin. It helps five enzymes that are key to processing fats, sugar and amino acids (the building blocks of protein).
plain.Folate is a water-soluble B vitamin that: Folate (vitamin B9) is a water-soluble B vitamin. The term covers natural food folates and folic acid, the form in supplements and fortified foods.
plain.Vitamin B12 is a water-soluble vitamin t: Vitamin B12 dissolves in water and contains the mineral cobalt, which is why its forms are called cobalamins.
plain.Choline is an essential nutrient that is: Choline is a nutrient you need from food. It supplies small carbon groups (methyl groups) your body uses in many chemical steps.
plain.Calcium, the most abundant mineral in th: Calcium is the most plentiful mineral in your body. It makes up much of your bones and teeth and keeps tissues strong but flexible so you can move.
plain.Iron is a mineral that is naturally pres: Iron is a key part of hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from your lungs to the rest of your body.
plain.Magnesium, an abundant mineral in the bo: Magnesium helps more than 300 enzyme systems, including ones for making protein, muscle and nerve function, blood sugar control and blood pressure.
plain.Phosphorus, an essential mineral, is nat: Phosphorus is a mineral that is part of your bones, teeth, DNA and RNA.
plain.Potassium, the most abundant intracellul: Potassium is the main positively charged mineral inside your cells. Every cell needs it to keep the right amount of fluid and electrical balance.
plain.Zinc, an essential mineral, is naturally: Zinc is an essential mineral found in some foods and supplements, and also in some cold lozenges, cold remedies and denture creams.
plain.Copper, an essential mineral, is natural: Copper is an essential mineral that helps several enzymes. They’re involved in making energy, using iron, building connective tissue, and making brain chemical messengers.
plain.Manganese is an essential trace element: Manganese is a trace mineral that many enzymes need, including the SOD enzyme in mitochondria (SOD2).
plain.Selenium is an essential mineral that is: Selenium is an essential mineral found in many foods and some supplements.
plain.Iodine is a trace element that is natura: Iodine is a trace mineral (found in some foods and iodized salt) that your thyroid uses to make its hormones, T4 and T3.
plain.The two major classes of polyunsaturated: Omega-3 and omega-6 are the two main types of polyunsaturated fats (PUFAs). Like all fats, they are long chains of carbon atoms.
plain.The classification indicates the strengt: The IARC group tells you how sure scientists are that something can cause cancer. It does not tell you how much your own risk goes up.
plain.The IARC classifications describe the st: IARC groups rate how strong the evidence is, not how big the risk is.
plain.In the case of processed meat, this clas: Processed meat is in Group 1 because studies of people show enough evidence that eating it causes colon and rectal cancer.
plain.An analysis of data from 10 studies esti: Across 10 studies, each extra 50 g of processed meat eaten a day raised colorectal cancer risk by about 18%. That is a relative increase, not an 18% chance of getting cancer.
plain.There is convincing evidence that consum: The evidence that processed meat causes colorectal cancer is rated “convincing”, the strongest level.
plain.In the case of red meat, the classificat: Red meat is in Group 2A (“probably”) because studies in people show a link with colorectal cancer, but the evidence is limited; lab studies show how it could happen.
plain.However, if the association of red meat: If red meat does cause colorectal cancer, each extra 100 g a day might raise risk by about 17% (a relative increase).
plain.Consumption of red meat is probably a ca: Eating red meat is rated as probably causing colorectal cancer.
plain.The International Agency for Research on: Alcohol has been in IARC Group 1 since 1987 because there is strong evidence it causes cancers of the mouth, throat, voice box, esophagus and liver.
plain.For example, women who have just one dri: Even one drink a day is linked to a higher breast cancer risk in women than less than one drink a week, and risk rises with heavier or binge drinking.
plain.There is strong evidence that consuming: Alcohol is strongly linked to higher risk of several cancers (mouth and throat, esophagus, breast after menopause, liver, colon and rectum) and probably stomach and pre-menopause breast cancer. It is probably linked to lower kidney cancer risk, but that is not a reason to drink.
plain.Exposure to aflatoxins is associated wit: Aflatoxins (toxins made by molds on some crops) are linked to a higher risk of liver cancer.
plain.there is strong evidence that consuming: Cantonese-style salted fish is strongly linked to a higher risk of cancer at the back of the nose and throat (nasopharynx).
plain.Drinking very hot beverages was classifi: Drinking very hot drinks is rated as probably causing cancer (Group 2A).
plain.The National Toxicology Program’s Report: Acrylamide is expected to cause cancer in humans, based on studies in lab animals given it in drinking water.
plain.Heterocyclic amines (HCAs) and polycycli: HCAs and PAHs are chemicals that form when meat, poultry or fish is cooked at high heat, like pan frying or grilling over a flame.
plain.The attributable risk of liver cancers i: Liver cancer caused by birth control pills is very rare: fewer than 1 case per million users.
plain.Incidence rates per 1000 women-years for: In a trial of women at high risk of breast cancer, uterine cancers were more common with tamoxifen than with placebo (for example 2.2 vs 0.71 endometrial cancers per 1,000 women per year).
plain.In the controlled portions of 39 global: Across 39 trials, lymphoma happened in 2 of 7,973 people on adalimumab and 1 of 4,848 people on comparison treatment.
plain.In addition, during the three year PROac: In a 3-year trial, bladder cancer was found in 0.54% of people on pioglitazone vs 0.19% on placebo.

ROS: Unstable, highly reactive molecules containing oxygen (such as superoxide and hydrogen peroxide). The body makes them during normal energy production; too many can damage cells.
free radical: A molecule with an unpaired (“unshared”) electron, which makes it unstable and quick to react with and damage other molecules.
oxidative stress: When reactive oxygen species build up faster than the body’s antioxidant defenses can handle them, which can damage cells.
oxidation: A chemical reaction where a molecule loses electrons, often by reacting with oxygen. Rusting and fats going rancid are everyday examples.
antioxidant: A substance that prevents or slows damage from free radicals, for example by giving up an electron or helping enzymes that remove them.
SOD: An enzyme the body makes that turns the superoxide radical into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide. Humans have SOD1 (copper/zinc, inside cells), SOD2 (manganese, in mitochondria) and SOD3 (copper/zinc, outside cells).
superoxide: A reactive oxygen species (O2•−) formed when oxygen picks up one extra electron, for example in mitochondria.
hydrogen peroxide: H2O2, a reactive oxygen molecule made by SOD; enzymes such as catalase and glutathione peroxidase turn it into water.
catalase: An enzyme that breaks hydrogen peroxide down into water and oxygen.
glutathione peroxidase: A family of selenium-containing enzymes that turn hydrogen peroxide and other peroxides into water or harmless alcohols.
glutathione reductase: An enzyme that recycles glutathione (an antioxidant) so it can be used again; it needs a form of riboflavin (FAD).
selenoprotein: A protein that contains selenium built into its structure. Humans have 25 of them.
enzyme: A protein that speeds up a specific chemical reaction in the body.
cofactor: A non-protein helper, often a mineral or vitamin, that an enzyme needs in order to work.
mitochondria: Tiny structures inside cells that turn food and oxygen into usable energy (singular: mitochondrion).
cytoplasm: The jelly-like fluid inside a cell, outside the nucleus.
extracellular: Outside the cells, for example in tissue spaces or blood.
myelination: Forming myelin, the fatty coating around nerve fibers that helps signals travel quickly.
collagen: The main structural protein in tendons, ligaments, skin, bone and cartilage. It gives them strength.
neurotransmitter: A chemical messenger nerve cells use to signal each other.
carotenoid: Yellow, orange and red plant pigments (like beta-carotene and lycopene). Some can be turned into vitamin A.
in vitro: Done in a test tube or lab dish, not in a living body.
DRI: The set of nutrient targets and limits from the U.S. National Academies; it includes the RDA, AI, UL and AMDR.
RDA: The daily amount that meets the needs of nearly all (97–98%) healthy people of a given age and sex.
AI: A daily amount assumed to be enough, used when there isn’t enough evidence to set an RDA.
UL: The highest daily amount unlikely to cause harm for almost everyone. It is a ceiling, not a goal.
AMDR: The range of calories from carbohydrate, fat and protein linked to lower chronic-disease risk while meeting nutrient needs.
EER: An estimate of daily calories needed to keep weight steady, based on age, sex, height, weight and activity.
BMI: Weight (kg) divided by height (m) squared. A screening number, not a diagnosis; it does not measure body fat directly.
IARC: International Agency for Research on Cancer
The WHO cancer agency. Its groups (1, 2A, 2B, 3) rate how strong the evidence is that something can cause cancer, not how big the risk is.
FNB: The National Academies board that sets the Dietary Reference Intakes.
ODS: The NIH office that publishes nutrient fact sheets used throughout this app.
CYP3A4: A liver and gut enzyme that breaks down many medicines. Grapefruit can block it, which can raise some drug levels.
INR: A blood test of how long blood takes to clot, used to monitor warfarin.
EGRAC: A blood test of riboflavin (vitamin B2) status.
FAD: An active form of riboflavin (vitamin B2) that many enzymes use.
AREDS: Large NIH trials of a supplement mix for age-related macular degeneration; also the name of that formula.
ORAC: A test-tube score of antioxidant power; it does not show effects in the human body.
macular degeneration: An eye disease that damages the center of the retina and blurs central vision.
hemorrhagic stroke: A stroke caused by bleeding in or around the brain.
DNA synthesis: Making new DNA, needed whenever a cell divides.
thymidylate: One of the four building blocks of DNA.
methylation: Adding a small carbon group (a methyl group) to a molecule; the body uses it to build and control many molecules.
peroxiredoxin: A family of enzymes that remove hydrogen peroxide.
macronutrient: Nutrients needed in large amounts that supply calories: carbohydrate, fat and protein.
micronutrient: Vitamins and minerals, needed in small amounts.
kcal: The “calorie” on food labels: a unit of food energy.
elastin: A stretchy protein that lets tissues like skin, blood vessels and lungs stretch and spring back.
tendon: A tough cord of tissue that connects a muscle to a bone.
ligament: A tough band of tissue that connects one bone to another at a joint.
cartilage: Firm, smooth, flexible tissue that cushions joints and shapes parts like the ears and nose.
fascia: Thin sheets of connective tissue that wrap and separate muscles and organs.
UV index: A daily forecast of how strong the sun’s ultraviolet rays are. 3 or higher means protect your skin.
PPE: Gear like gloves, goggles, face shields, respirators and lab coats that reduces contact with hazards.
hypothermia: Body temperature dropping too low (below 95°F / 35°C). It is a medical emergency.
frostbite: Skin and tissue that freezes, usually on fingers, toes, nose, ears or cheeks.
heat stroke: The most serious heat illness: the body can no longer cool itself. Call 911.
hypoxia: Not enough oxygen reaching the body’s tissues, for example at high altitude.

learn.title: Free radicals, oxidative stress and antioxidants
body: Some molecules, called free radicals, have an unpaired electron. That makes them unstable, so they react with nearby molecules and can damage fats, proteins and DNA.
Your body makes reactive oxygen species (ROS), including some free radicals, every day while turning food into energy. Small amounts are normal and even used as signals.
Oxidative stress means ROS are building up faster than your defenses can handle them.

Defenses include enzymes your body makes (like SOD, catalase and glutathione peroxidase, which need minerals such as copper, zinc, manganese and selenium) and antioxidants from food (like vitamins C and E).
More is not always better: high-dose antioxidant pills have caused harm in some trials (see Cellular › Cautions).

learn.title: SOD (superoxide dismutase)
body: SOD is an enzyme your body makes. It turns superoxide, a free radical, into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide; catalase and glutathione peroxidases then turn hydrogen peroxide into water.
Humans have three forms: SOD1 (copper and zinc, inside cells), SOD2 (manganese, inside mitochondria) and SOD3 (copper and zinc, outside cells).

That is why copper, zinc and manganese matter for this defense. SOD is a protein, and proteins you swallow are easily broken down in the gut, so SOD pills are not a reliable way to raise SOD in your cells.

learn.title: What DRI, RDA, AI, UL and AMDR mean
body: DRI (Dietary Reference Intakes) is the family of nutrient targets set by the U.S. National Academies.
RDA: the daily amount that covers nearly all healthy people. AI: a best-estimate amount used when there isn’t enough data for an RDA.
UL: the upper limit, the most you can take daily with little risk of harm. It is a ceiling, not a goal; most ULs apply to supplements plus food.
AMDR: healthy ranges for the share of calories from carbs (45–65%), fat (20–35%) and protein (10–35%) for adults.
This app shows your intake as a % of your RDA or AI, based on your age group and sex.

learn.title: How to read source badges and evidence tiers
body: Every claim links to a source badge. Tap a badge to see the title, publisher, date and link.

Each small gray badge reads source · year · tier, for example “NIH 2021 · T2”. Tap it for full details. The tier (T1–T4) is shown in blue-slate text, darker = stronger evidence: T1 official guidelines, FDA labeling, systematic reviews/meta-analyses · T2 randomized trials and authoritative government summaries (NIH ODS, MedlinePlus) · T3 observational/cohort studies · T4 case reports, narrative reviews, lab/animal studies or expert opinion.

The year is when the source was published or last updated, with 4 tiny bars for freshness: 4 bars = 5 years or newer, 3 = 5–10 years, 2 = 10–15 years, 1 = older than 15 years, ? = date unknown. Older is not automatically wrong; it just means newer research may exist.
Badge colors never mean “good” or “bad” for your body. Only the green coverage ring and the colored body overlays show body scores.
Quotes are copied word-for-word from the source. The “In plain words” lines only restate the quote in simpler language.

learn.title: How food–drug interactions work
body: Some foods change how your body absorbs, breaks down or responds to a medicine.
A well-known example is grapefruit: it can block an enzyme (CYP3A4) that breaks down some drugs, so more of the drug stays in your blood. That is why some labels warn against grapefruit.
Others work differently, for example vitamin K-rich foods and warfarin.
Never start, stop or change a medicine based on this app. Ask your pharmacist or prescriber.

learn.title: IARC cancer groups vs. your actual risk
body: IARC (the WHO cancer agency) sorts agents into groups by how strong the evidence is that they can cause cancer: Group 1 (carcinogenic to humans), 2A (probably), 2B (possibly), 3 (not classifiable).
The group says how sure scientists are, not how dangerous something is. Processed meat and tobacco are both Group 1, but the risk from tobacco is far larger.
Your own risk depends on how much, how often and for how long, plus many other factors.

evidence.q: Superoxide dismutases (SODs) are universal enzymes of organisms that live in the presence of oxygen. They catalyze the conversion of superoxide into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide.
evidence.p: SOD is a helper protein (enzyme) that living things using oxygen make themselves. It turns superoxide, a very reactive “free radical”, into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide.

evidence.q: The catalase (CAT), glutathione peroxidases (GPXs), and PRXs convert H2O2 into water.
evidence.p: Hydrogen peroxide is then handled by other enzymes, catalase and glutathione peroxidases (and peroxiredoxins), which turn it into water.

evidence.q: The Cu/Zn SOD SOD1 is the cytoplasmic isoform but has also been identified in the nucleus, lysosome, peroxisome, and the mitochondrial intermembrane space.
evidence.p: SOD1 uses copper and zinc and works mainly in the fluid inside cells (the cytoplasm).

evidence.q: The Mn SOD SOD2 localizes to the mitochondrial matrix.
evidence.p: SOD2 uses manganese and works inside mitochondria, the cell’s energy factories, where a lot of superoxide is made.

evidence.q: The Cu/Zn SOD SOD3 is secreted into the extracellular space.
evidence.p: SOD3 also uses copper and zinc, but it is sent outside cells, into the spaces between them and fluids like blood.

evidence.q: Oral administration of protein is very challenging for therapeutic applications due to its instability and easy degradation in the gastrointestinal tract.
evidence.p: SOD is a protein. Proteins you swallow tend to be broken down in the stomach and gut, so an SOD pill is unlikely to arrive in your cells as working SOD. Your body makes its own SOD; what it needs from food is copper, zinc and manganese.
